items.title: Indeterminate forms and why limits need techniques
items.text: Four forms — 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞ − ∞ and 0 × ∞ — are the signal that plain substitution has failed and a technique is needed. Reach for this first: name the form before you choose a tool, and remember a reciprocal turns the first, second and fourth into one another.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L$$

items.title: Factorisation method for 0/0
items.text: When substitution gives 0/0, factorise the top and the bottom and cancel the common factor, which is a tiny non-zero quantity rather than a zero, then substitute. This is the first tool to try on any polynomial 0/0 limit.

items.title: Rationalisation method for 0/0
items.text: The moment a 0/0 limit shows a root sign there is nothing to factorise, so multiply by the conjugate and let the difference of two squares destroy the surd. Roots on both top and bottom need both conjugates in the same line.

items.title: Finding a and b when the limit value is given
items.text: If the denominator goes to 0 and the limit is a finite number, the numerator is forced to go to 0 as well, and that is the equation students miss. Use it whenever the answer is handed to you and two unknowns have to be found.

items.title: Practice: factorisation and rationalisation limits
items.text: Two board-level 0/0 limits to attempt with your own pen: one rationalisation, and one where the given limit 5 pins a = 24. The second also answers the standing doubt — how can 0/0 come out as 5.
f: $$\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = L \;\text{with}\; f(c)=g(c)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{cancel } (x-c) \text{ first, then put } x=c$$

groups.sub: The infinity forms: ∞/∞, ∞ − ∞ and limits at minus infinity

items.title: The ∞/∞ form: divide by the highest power
items.text: For ∞/∞, divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of x on show; every leftover term with x underneath dies to 0 and what survives is the answer. You want an infinity in the denominator, because anything finite over infinity goes to 0.

items.title: ∞/∞ with exponential terms
items.text: Same method, except the largest infinity now hides in the base: divide top and bottom by the largest base raised to x. Every leftover proper fraction to the power x dies to 0.

items.title: When the powers are unequal: answer 0 or infinity
items.text: Do not memorise a rule for unequal degrees. Divide by the highest power you can see and the answer declares itself as 0 or as ±∞, with the sign of the leftover denominator deciding which infinity.

items.title: Practice: three ∞/∞ limits
items.text: Three ∞/∞ limits in a minute, with one move each. The same division by the highest power produces a ratio, a 0 and an infinity, which is the point of the set.
f: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a_m x^m + \cdots}{b_n x^n + \cdots} = \frac{a_m}{b_n} \ \text{if } m = n, \quad 0 \ \text{if } m < n, \quad \infty \ \text{if } m > n$$

items.title: ∞/∞ when the polynomial is already factored
items.text: When both sides are already in brackets, do not expand: count the degree and split that power of n across the brackets one at a time. Cubic over cubic leaves only the ratio of the leading coefficients.

items.title: The ∞ − ∞ form: rationalise first
items.text: Two roots running off to infinity leave nothing to cancel, so multiply by the conjugate to turn ∞ − ∞ into ∞/∞ and then divide by x. Remember that dividing a root by x means dividing everything inside it by x squared.

items.title: Limits as x → −∞: substitute x = −t
items.text: Put x = −t so that t runs to plus infinity, work the whole question in t, and the sign can never go wrong. This is the one place where a careless square root turns a sure mark into a lost one.

items.title: Existence of a limit: (x² + 1)/(x + 1) − (ax − b)
items.text: Take the LCM, write the numerator in systematic powers of x, and kill the coefficient of x squared, which is the only way the limit can be finite. The surviving x coefficient then equals the given value, giving a = 1 and b = 6.

items.title: Practice: limit existence quiz and bonus problems
items.text: The same existence question with the limit pinned at 4: kill the x squared coefficient for a = 1, then read the x coefficient to get b = 5. Nothing new is needed, only careful bracket multiplication.

items.title: Limits of the form (aⁿ + bⁿ) to the power 1/n: take the largest term common
items.text: Take the largest base common and the answer is simply that largest base, because every leftover proper fraction raised to the power n dies. It works for any number of terms.

items.title: Road map: standard limits and the algebraic limit formula
items.text: After the three basic techniques come the standard limits, where you know the answer because there is a formula. The algebraic one is the first of them, and it fires the moment you see a difference of equal powers over x − a.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule
items.text: If the limit sits in 0/0 or ∞/∞, differentiate the top alone and the bottom alone, substitute again, and repeat until a finite value appears. There is no quotient rule anywhere in this.

items.title: Practice: five L'Hôpital questions
items.text: Five algebraic 0/0 limits, each finished by differentiating top and bottom once. The point of the set is speed: L'Hôpital beats factorising on every one of them.

groups.sub: Trigonometric limits: the heart of the chapter

items.title: The two trigonometric limit formulas
items.text: Sine of something over that same something goes to 1, and so does tangent of something over the same something, provided the something itself goes to 0. The whole of trigonometric limits rests on these two lines.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin f(x)}{f(x)} = 1, \quad \text{provided } f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to a$$
$$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\tan f(x)}{f(x)} = 1, \quad \text{provided } f(x) \to 0 \text{ as } x \to a$$

items.title: Forcing 'something' to approach zero
items.text: If the angle inside the sine does not go to 0 on its own, rewrite it until it does, then match the denominator to it. Factorising, or an identity such as cos x = sin(90 degrees − x), is usually all it takes.

items.title: Shortcut: the coefficient of x is the answer
items.text: For sin(ax)/x as x goes to 0 the answer is just a, and the same holds for tan(ax). Use it to skip the multiply-and-divide step for good.

items.title: Using the coefficient shortcut
items.text: Divide the whole fraction above and below by x, read off the coefficient of x inside each sine and tangent, and the answer appears. Powers come along for the ride: cube the bracket's limit.
f: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin ax - \tan bx}{\sin cx + \tan dx} = \frac{a - b}{c + d}$$

items.title: The only two trigonometric identities a limit needs
items.text: Almost every trigonometric limit runs on 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin squared x and on the difference of two cosines as a product of two sines. Learn these two and most of these limits stop being trigonometry.

items.title: Why splitting a limit by x is legal
items.text: A limit splits across a product or a quotient only once every piece has a finite limit and no indeterminate form is left. That rule is the whole licence behind the divide-by-x shortcut.

items.title: Standard 1 − cos questions
items.text: Write 1 − cos of an angle as twice the sine squared of half that angle, then read the coefficients. The standard results 1 − cos mx over x squared and the difference of two cosines over x squared are worth keeping by heart.

items.title: Oral practice: degrees, and 1 − cos in one line
items.text: Convert degrees into radians before any limit formula touches the question, which is why sine of x degrees over x gives pi over 180. Every 1 − cos question then finishes in one line.

items.title: Oral practice: mixed sine and tan limits
items.text: For a ratio of sines and tangents at x going to 0, divide every term by x and read off the coefficients. If you have to multiply anything out, the question has already cost you too long.

items.title: How the trigonometric-limit toolkit fits together
items.text: Everything so far is one statement used faster and faster: sine of something over that same something goes to 1. Walk back through the path before you take on the harder questions.

items.title: Sine of infinity, and the 0 × ∞ form
items.text: Sine of infinity is an unknown bounded value between −1 and 1, never an infinity, so a bounded numerator over something blowing up goes to 0. A 0 × ∞ form must still be flipped into 0/0 before any formula applies.

items.title: Limits at infinity containing a sine
items.text: Check the format in the first three seconds: a bounded sine over x goes to 0, while x times sine of 1 over x is a 0 × ∞ that rearranges into the standard form and gives 1. The two look like twins and land on different answers.

items.title: Sine x over x equals 1 only when x → 0
items.text: The formula needs the angle itself to go to 0. Anywhere else there is no indeterminate form at all, so you simply substitute, and at x going to pi over 2 the value is 2 over pi.

items.title: When a side identity is needed
items.text: Two identities carry nearly every question, but the difference of two sines as a product does turn up often enough to be worth knowing. Keep it as the third card in the pack, not the first.

items.title: The classic (tan x − sin x) over x cubed
items.text: Write tangent as sine over cosine, take sine x out, replace 1 − cos x by twice the sine squared of the half angle, and the answer is one half. This is the single most likely trigonometric limit to appear in a paper.

items.title: Subjective IIT question with tan 2θ
items.text: Expand tan 2x as twice tan x over 1 minus tan squared x so the numerator collapses to a cube, write the squared bracket below as four sine to the fourth, then divide by x to the fourth. Two identities and one division finish an old subjective paper question.

items.title: Two harder manipulations at pi over 2 and pi over 6
items.text: Both of these are the same trick in different clothes: force the question into sine of something over that same something, with the something going to 0. Writing a sine plus b cosine as one sine is the move that cracks the second.

items.title: Substituting x = a ± h to reach h → 0
items.text: When nothing clicks at x going to a, put x = a + h or x = a − h so that h goes to 0 and every standard formula applies again. Plus h is the right-hand limit, minus h the left-hand limit, and the substitution goes into the whole expression at once.

items.title: The pi over 2 ± h substitution in action
items.text: One substitution turns a heavy-looking limit at pi over 2 into a sine squared over a sine, which one division by h finishes. Both sides come out as 0, so the limit exists.

items.title: Greatest integer with trigonometric limits
items.text: Near 0, sine x over x creeps up to 1 from below while tangent x over x comes down to 1 from above. A greatest integer bracket inside the limit therefore gives 0 and 1, while a bracket outside the limit gives 1 and 1.

items.title: Greatest integer questions solved
items.text: Never take the floor of the limit value. Decide whether the expression is sitting just below or just above the integer, and floor that, which is why x over tan x gives 0 and x over sin x gives 1.

groups.sub: Logarithmic and exponential limits, and the 1 to the power ∞ form

items.title: Logarithmic limits: ln(1 + something) over the same something
items.text: Natural log of 1 plus something, over that same something, goes to 1 whenever the something goes to 0. That single formula is the whole of logarithmic limits, and the coefficient shortcut applies to it too.

items.title: Base changing theorem for log limits
items.text: The formula only works in base e, so convert any other base first with log to base b of a written as ln a over ln b. A base 3 logarithm simply leaves a clean 1 over ln 3 outside.

items.title: Log limits: forcing ln(1 + something) over the same something
items.text: Every log limit has to be forced into the standard shape with the same quantity inside the bracket and underneath. Add and subtract 1 inside the log, or split the constant out with the log of a product, then divide by whatever that quantity is.

items.title: ln(cos 2x) over tan squared 3x: adding and subtracting 1 inside the log
items.text: Write cos 2x as 1 plus (cos 2x − 1) so the standard log limit becomes 1, and what is left is an old trigonometric limit giving −2 over 9. Use this whenever there is no 1 inside the logarithm anywhere.

items.title: Quiz solutions: log limits mixed with 1 − cos x
items.text: Turn the logarithm into the standard shape and 1 − cos into a sine squared, then divide top and bottom by x squared. Three quiz questions in three costumes, all the same two lines.

items.title: Why you cannot split a limit: the ∞ − ∞ trap
items.text: Substitute into the whole expression at once. Splitting this one into two pieces makes each piece infinite, creates an ∞ − ∞ form, and produces the false answer 0.

items.title: IIT subjective problem with ln(1 + 2h) and 2 ln(1 + h)
items.text: Pull the coefficient inside as a power, merge the two logarithms into one, add and subtract 1 inside it, and force the denominator to become the same quantity. The limit is −1.

items.title: Exponential limits: (a to the x, minus 1) over x goes to ln a
items.text: One formula covers the whole topic, and with base e it becomes 1. In general, e to the something minus 1, over that same something, goes to 1 as the something goes to 0.

items.title: Exponential limit problems: common base, sine squared and factorisation
items.text: Force the standard shape every time: take the smaller base common to manufacture the 1, give every block exactly the same quantity underneath it, and factorise a product of two brackets when the numerator allows it. The last one comes out as ln a times ln b.

items.title: (e to the cos 2x, minus e) over tan squared 3x: taking e common first
items.text: If the numerator is not already e to the something minus 1, pull the constant e out first and then force the standard shape. The trigonometric limits finish it at −2e over 9.

items.title: The 1 to the power ∞ form: λ = lim (base − 1) × power, answer e to the λ
items.text: Confirm the base goes to 1 and the power goes to infinity, then compute λ as the limit of (base − 1) times the power. The answer is e to the λ, never λ on its own, and writing λ alone is a lost mark.

items.title: Three 1 to the power ∞ problems solved
items.text: With a rational base, take the LCM in (base − 1), multiply by the power, and settle the leftover ∞/∞ by comparing coefficients of x. That value is λ and the answer is e to the λ.

items.title: Revision: the seven indeterminate forms and the technique for each
items.text: Seven forms and a fixed tool for each: factorise or rationalise for 0/0, divide by the biggest infinity for ∞/∞, an LCM or a conjugate for ∞ − ∞, the λ formula for 1 to the power ∞, and a reciprocal to convert 0 × ∞. Name the form and the tool is already decided.
f: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a_n x^n + \cdots}{b_m x^m + \cdots} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{divide numerator and denominator by } x^{\max(n,m)}$$

groups.sub: Standard expansions, coefficient matching, and L'Hôpital again

items.title: Standard expansions you must memorise
items.text: Six series — sine, cosine, tangent, e to the x, log of 1 plus x, and the binomial — are the whole toolkit for expansion limits. Each one carries its own range of x where it is legal, and the tangent series has plain denominators rather than factorials.

items.title: Remembering the expansions, and rescaling them
items.text: Rebuild any series from three facts: odd or even, its value at 0, and the alternating factorial pattern. For sine 2x or e to the minus x, substitute into the standard series instead of memorising a new one.

items.title: Expansion limits: match the minimum power, read off the coefficient
items.text: Once expanded, every such limit is a polynomial over a polynomial. For a finite non-zero limit the minimum power on top equals the minimum power below, and the answer is the ratio of those two coefficients, so every higher power is a waste of ink.
f: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{4} + b x^{5} + c x^{6}}{\alpha x^{4} + \beta x^{7} + \gamma x^{9}} = \frac{a}{\alpha}$$
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{m} + \cdots}{\alpha x^{n} + \cdots} = \begin{cases} a/\alpha & m = n \\ 0 & m > n \\ \text{undefined} & m < n \end{cases}$$

items.title: Four expansion problems done by coefficient-picking
items.text: Expansion is the right tool when two functions are added and cannot be combined, so nothing can be taken common or cancelled. Expand each one, pick only the coefficient of the power that matches the denominator, and that coefficient is the limit.
f: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)}{x^n} = \text{coefficient of } x^n \text{ in the expansion of } f(x)$$

items.title: When the coefficient vanishes: zero and undefined limits
items.text: Compare the lowest surviving power on top with the power below: bigger gives 0, equal gives the ratio of the two coefficients, and smaller means there is no finite limit. The setter has already arranged for one of the first two, so a third outcome means recheck your expansion.

items.title: Finding a, b and c from a given expansion limit
items.text: Expand every term only as far as the power sitting in the denominator, force all the lower-power coefficients to zero, and set the matching coefficient equal to the given limit. These are the four-mark questions most of a class leaves blank.

items.title: Expansion limits that need the binomial expansion
items.text: One binomial expansion handles every bracket-with-a-power limit, for any index, fractional or negative. With x squared below, the whole answer is a single coefficient: the index term times the square of the bracket's x coefficient.

items.title: L'Hôpital's rule: two limits nothing else cracks
items.text: Reach for L'Hôpital when a long division or an unknown expansion would otherwise be needed, such as a fractional power in the denominator or a logarithm over a power of x. Both of those fall in one line.

items.title: Quiz: four limits to do by L'Hôpital's rule
items.text: Four limits you could expand, deliberately set to be done by differentiating top and bottom. Confirm the form first, every time.

items.title: Quiz solutions, and differentiating with respect to the right variable
items.text: Whatever the arrow starts from is the variable and whatever it points to is a constant, so in a limit as alpha goes to beta you differentiate with respect to alpha only. Stop applying the rule the moment a standard limit appears.

groups.sub: Continuity at a point, and the standard traps

items.title: Continuity at a point: LHL = RHL = f(a)
items.text: A function is continuous at a only when the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value f(a) are all equal and all finite. If you know limits you already know continuity: it is three numbers and one condition.

items.title: Continuity of piecewise-defined functions
items.text: Test three things at the point: the rule just below it, the rule just above it, and the rule exactly at it. The only skill is reading which line of the definition owns which side.

items.title: 1/x and e to the 1/x at x = 0: the LHL and RHL trap
items.text: 1/x runs to plus infinity from the right and minus infinity from the left, so e to the 1/x blows up on one side and dies on the other. On the right-hand side the form is ∞/∞, so divide top and bottom by e to the 1/x.

items.title: Quiz: continuity with e to the 1/x, greatest integer, and a bonus k
items.text: Three continuity questions to attempt alone: another e to the 1/x function, a greatest-integer function, and one where the value of k has to be found. Attempt all three unaided — that is the point.

items.title: Quiz solutions: finding k, the 0 over ∞ form, and [x] + [−x]
items.text: Each one is either a limit set equal to f(a) or a function you build from both sides: k = 1 for the first, x over 1 plus e to the 1/x is continuous at 0, and [x] + [−x] breaks only at the integers. A form that looks indeterminate is not always indeterminate.

items.title: Fixing constants by continuity: cot 4x over cot 2x, and f at pi over 4
items.text: Flip a ratio of cotangents into tangents and it collapses to the ratio of the angles. When a function is continuous on an open interval its value at an interior point is forced to equal the limit there, found fastest by L'Hôpital.

items.title: Only the change points can break continuity
items.text: A piecewise function can only break where its definition changes, so there are never more than a handful of suspects. Make the two values agree at each of those points and the function is continuous on the whole interval.

items.title: Continuity of [x] times x squared: define the function yourself
items.text: Replace the greatest integer by the constant it equals on each unit interval, which turns the problem into an ordinary piecewise function. Then test only the change points, and here only two of them break.

items.title: End points: one-sided continuity
items.text: At the left end of the domain you check right-continuity only, and at the right end left-continuity only, because the other side does not exist. That makes end points the easiest points in the chapter.

items.title: A limit does not need an indeterminate form
items.text: If substitution gives a finite defined value, that value is the limit and no method is needed. Carrying the belief that a limit only happens when 0/0 appears is what makes easy continuity questions look like traps.

groups.sub: The discontinuity taxonomy, greatest integer and composite functions

items.title: Removable versus irremovable discontinuity, and why the names
items.text: Removable means the limit at the point exists but does not equal f(a), so one redefinition repairs it. Irremovable means the one-sided limits disagree, and no single value can sit in that gap.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \text{ exists, but } \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \neq f(a)$$

items.title: Isolated-point and missing-point discontinuity
items.text: Removable splits in two: isolated point, where f(a) exists but differs from the limit, and missing point, where f(a) is not defined at all. Both graphs have a hole; only one has the extra dot.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L, \quad f(a) \text{ exists}, \quad f(a) \neq L$$

items.title: Irremovable: jump and oscillating discontinuity
items.text: If both one-sided limits are finite but unequal you have a jump. If a one-sided limit does not exist at all, as with sine of 1 over x near 0, the discontinuity is essential and the function oscillates rather than settles.
f: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = L_1, \quad \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L_2, \quad L_1 \neq L_2$$
$$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \ \text{or} \ \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) \ \text{does not exist}$$

items.title: Type 1: continuity questions that are two limits in disguise
items.text: The question says continuity, but nothing about continuity happens: you evaluate two limits and match them to f(0). Write the LHL = RHL = f(a) line first, every time.

items.title: Type 2 set-up: sum of the points where [x² − x + 3] is discontinuous
items.text: A quadratic locked inside a greatest integer bracket on a closed interval, asking for the sum of the break points. The first move is always to graph the quadratic, never to stare at the bracket.
f: $$\lfloor t \rfloor = \text{the greatest integer less than or equal to } t$$
$$g(x) \in \mathbb{Z} \;\Rightarrow\; \lfloor g(x) \rfloor \text{ may jump at that } x$$

items.title: Graphing the quadratic on [−1, 2]: vertex and end values
items.text: Three numbers fix the whole picture: the vertex from minus b over 2a and minus the discriminant over 4a, plus the two end values. You never need a table of twenty points.

items.title: Greatest integer of the quadratic: building the step graph
items.text: Ask one question at each integer level — where does the curve touch it — and the greatest-integer graph becomes a staircase of flat steps with a break at each crossing. The curve falls from 5 to 2.75 and climbs back to 5, so it can only touch 3, 4 and 5.

items.title: The points of discontinuity and their sum
items.text: You never need the two irrational break points themselves: the sum of the roots of the quadratic set equal to 4 gives their total in one line. Count the two end points, where one-sided continuity also fails, and the sum is 3.

items.title: Why greatest-integer questions are really about range
items.text: A greatest-integer question is a range question in disguise: find what the inside expression ranges over, and read each step as the integer included and the next one excluded. At an exact integer the value belongs to the new step.

items.title: Final answer 3, and why the graph was essential
items.text: The closing step is pure addition, but every term in that sum was read off the picture. Without the graph you cannot know that the curve runs from 2.75 up to 5 and so touches only three integer levels.

items.title: Continuity of a composite function f(g(x)) at a point
items.text: Never build the composite. Find the three limiting values of g at the point, feed each into f, and compare the three answers, which takes well under a minute.
f: $$f(g(x))\ \text{is continuous at } x=a \iff \lim_{x\to a^-} f(g(x)) = \lim_{x\to a^+} f(g(x)) = f(g(a))$$
$$\lim_{x\to a^+} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^+)\right), \qquad \lim_{x\to a^-} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^-)\right)$$

items.title: Quiz: continuity of fog with a signum function
items.text: Even when the inner function jumps at the point, the composite can still be continuous there. Compute all three values honestly and compare: here all three come out as plus one.

items.title: Wherever the denominator is zero the function is discontinuous
items.text: A zero on the bottom with a non-zero top puts the point outside the domain, so the function is discontinuous there and no one-sided limits are needed. Equal infinite one-sided limits still count as discontinuous, because infinity is not a value.

items.title: Points of discontinuity of fog: the inner-function trap
items.text: The simplified denominator is only half the answer. Every point where the inner function itself blows up must be added, because the cancellation that simplified the composite is meaningless there.

items.title: Discontinuity of f(f(x)) with f(x) = 1 over (1 − x)
items.text: The same trap in a new costume: x = 1 kills the inner function and x = 0 kills the simplified form, so both are points of discontinuity. A student who only simplifies hands in half the answer.

groups.sub: Differentiability, and the three question archetypes

items.title: Slope of the chord AB and what happens as h → 0
items.text: The chord joining the point and its neighbour h away has slope given by the difference quotient, whose denominator always collapses to h. Push the second point onto the first and the chord becomes the tangent.
f: $$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h} = \text{slope of the tangent at } A$$

items.title: Derivative at a point means slope of the tangent (first principle)
items.text: The derivative at a point is nothing but the slope of the tangent there, and the first-principles limit is exactly that slope. Keep the difference-of-sines identity to hand for a first-principles proof on a trigonometric function.

items.title: Right hand derivative and left hand derivative
items.text: Approaching from the right gives the right hand derivative, and writing minus h in place of h — in the denominator too — gives the left hand derivative, with h positive in both. The familiar first principle covers only the right-hand half.

items.title: Differentiability means a unique tangent
The two conditions for differentiability at a point
items.text: Differentiable at a means continuous at a and the two one-sided derivatives equal. Check continuity first, because a break in the graph makes the function non-differentiable whatever the derivatives do.
f: $$f \text{ differentiable at } x=a \iff f \text{ continuous at } x=a \ \text{ and } \ f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$
$$f \text{ discontinuous at } x=a \implies f \text{ non-differentiable at } x=a$$

items.title: Equal RHD and LHD cannot save a discontinuous graph
items.text: Two perfectly parallel tangents at a broken point still mean non-differentiable. Equal one-sided derivatives prove nothing until continuity has been confirmed.

items.title: The shortcut: differentiate each piece and put the point in
items.text: Check continuity, then differentiate the piece valid above the point and substitute for the right hand derivative, and the piece valid below it for the left. This clears most differentiability questions in three lines instead of two limits.

items.title: Worked example: a piecewise function that is differentiable at x = 1
items.text: Two different parabolas joined at x = 1: both give the value 9 and both derivatives give 5, so the join is smooth and the function is differentiable there. Value first, slope second.

items.title: Same derivatives but discontinuous: always check continuity first
items.text: Change one constant in the previous question and the answer flips, while the two derivatives do not change at all. Once you find a jump, stop — the answer is already non-differentiable.
f: $$f \text{ discontinuous at } x=a \;\Longrightarrow\; f \text{ not differentiable at } x=a$$
$$\text{LHD}=\text{RHD}=5 \quad\text{and yet } f \text{ is non-differentiable at } x=1$$

items.title: The three cases side by side
items.text: Differentiability needs one unique tangent, so continuity is step one and equal one-sided derivatives step two. Failing either one kills it, and the three cases laid side by side show how a broken graph can still have matching slopes.

items.title: Oral practice: checking differentiability at x = −1
items.text: Two numbers to match for continuity, two more for the derivatives, and the question is done without a single limit written out. Both pieces give 0 and both derivatives give 2, so it is differentiable.

items.title: Practice set: finding constants for continuity and differentiability
items.text: Two unknown constants at a joining point need two equations: one from continuity and one from equal one-sided derivatives. The letters inside the function make it look harder than the two lines it takes.

items.title: Quiz solutions: shortest route and the time-waster
items.text: Matching the derivatives of the two pieces at the junction usually drops one constant out immediately. And once the two one-sided limits disagree, stop: there is nothing left to differentiate.
f: $$f \text{ discontinuous at } c \Rightarrow f \text{ not differentiable at } c$$

items.title: Type 2: defining the function piecewise yourself (modulus)
items.text: Nobody hands you the two pieces for a modulus function, so split it at the point where the inside becomes zero and Type 2 turns into Type 1. The slopes are plus one on the right and minus one on the left, so the function is continuous but not differentiable at that point.
f: $$|x - a| = \begin{cases} x - a, & x \ge a \\ -(x - a), & x < a \end{cases}$$

items.title: The three types of continuity and differentiability questions
items.text: Every question in this topic is one of three: the piecewise function is given, you have to build it yourself, or you have to go back to the one-sided derivative definition. Knowing the type means your first step is never a guess.

items.title: Category 2 problems: define the function, then find LHD and RHD
items.text: Open the modulus, greatest integer or fractional part around the point first, and only then differentiate. The fractional part is always x minus the greatest integer, and between two integers the bracket is only a constant.

items.title: RHD and LHD of e to the mod x, mod x plus sine mod x, and mod x plus cosine mod x, at x = 0
items.text: Cosine is even so the modulus inside it can be dropped, while sine is odd so it must be split. All three functions come out continuous but non-differentiable at 0, with one-sided derivatives 1 and −1, 2 and −2, 1 and −1.

items.title: (x − 2) times mod(x² − 4): differentiable at 2 but not at −2
items.text: At x = 2 the factor (x − 2) is repeated, which flattens the corner so both one-sided derivatives are 0 and the function is differentiable. At x = −2 the two branches give plus and minus 16, so it is continuous but not differentiable.
f: $$f'(c^-) = f'(c^+) \iff f \text{ is differentiable at } x=c$$

items.title: x squared times [x]: one-sided derivatives at x = −1, 0, 1 and 2
items.text: On each side of an integer replace the bracket by its constant value and differentiate. The function breaks at every integer except 0, where the x squared switches the jump off and it is both continuous and differentiable.

items.title: Greatest integer with fractional part: 2[x] + 3{x} − 7x² at x = 0 and 1
items.text: Replace the bracket by its constant value and the fractional part by x minus the bracket on each interval, then work from the definition at the point. Continuity fails at both x = 0 and x = 1, so the function is non-differentiable there; whether the two one-sided derivatives genuinely agree or one of them diverges is flagged for a teacher to settle.

items.title: Algebra of continuity and differentiability for f ± g, fg and f over g
items.text: Continuous plus continuous stays continuous, and so does the quotient wherever the denominator is non-zero. Continuous plus discontinuous is always discontinuous, continuous times discontinuous can still be continuous when the continuous limit is 0, and if both are discontinuous nothing can be said.
f: $$f,\ g \text{ continuous at } a \;\Rightarrow\; f \pm g,\; fg \text{ continuous at } a$$
$$f,\ g \text{ continuous at } a,\ g(a) \neq 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{f}{g} \text{ continuous at } a$$
$$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x)g(x) = 0 = \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x)g(x)$$

items.title: Old IIT MCQ: which function is differentiable at x = 0, by inspection
items.text: Cosine of mod x is just cosine x, so two options die in five seconds without defining anything piecewise. Only the sine of mod x options need real work, and the difference of sine mod x and mod x is the differentiable one.
f: $$g \text{ differentiable},\; h \text{ not} \;\Rightarrow\; g \pm h \text{ not differentiable}$$

items.title: Category 3: derivative-looking limits solved by L'Hôpital, not by definition
items.text: When a limit looks like a derivative but is plain 0/0, do not reach for the definition: confirm the form and differentiate with respect to h. Remember that f(a) is a constant whose derivative is 0, and that the chain rule applies to the moving part.

items.title: Quiz: a symmetric difference quotient, and the chain-rule sign trap
items.text: The derivative of f(5 − t) with respect to t carries a factor of minus one, so the two terms add rather than cancel and the limit is f dashed at 5, not 0. Forget that sign and the wrong option is waiting for you.

items.title: Why the first-principles definition has not been needed so far
items.text: Every standard derivative formula was itself built from the one-sided derivative definition, which is why direct differentiation has been enough. The definition is the fallback, not the routine.
f: $$f'(a^{-}) = f'(a^{+}) = \text{finite} \iff f \text{ is differentiable at } x = a$$

items.title: x squared times sine of 1 over x, at x = 0: when you must go back to the definition
items.text: The direct derivative collapses into a cosine of 1 over x at 0, which has no value, so the formula failing proves nothing. Go back to the definition: a vanishing factor times a bounded one gives 0, so both one-sided derivatives are 0 and the function is differentiable.

items.title: Contrast: x times sine of 1 over x is continuous but non-differentiable at 0
items.text: Drop the square and the difference quotient becomes sine of 1 over h, which oscillates between −1 and 1 and has no limit. One surviving factor of h is the whole difference between differentiable and not.
